title: Congress Demands Manipur Chief Minister Quit and Fresh Polls as Violence Renews
excerpt: Citing 306 dead since May 2023 and the October 19 killing of three civilians, the party wants the Assembly dissolved, time-bound investigations and a roadmap for the displaced to go home.
body:
• The Congress party on October 25 demanded the resignation of Manipur Chief Minister Y. Khemchand Singh, dissolution of the state Assembly and fresh elections.
  • The party cites a toll of at least 306 dead since May 2023, about 60,000 displaced and 24,000 still unable to return home, with 49 people missing.
  • The immediate trigger is renewed violence: three Meitei civilians were killed on October 19, and protesters marching toward Lok Bhavan on October 23 were met with lathi charges and tear gas.
  • Congress also wants time-bound investigations, a review of the Suspension of Operations agreement, restored free movement and a rehabilitation roadmap.

The Congress party on Sunday demanded the immediate resignation of Manipur Chief Minister Y. Khemchand Singh, the dissolution of the state Assembly and fresh elections, accusing the BJP government of failing to stop more than three years of ethnic violence. At a press conference in New Delhi, Congress MP Saptagiri Ulaka said the conflict has claimed at least 306 lives since May 2023, displaced approximately 60,000 people — 24,000 of whom still cannot return home — and left 49 people missing, according to NEWire's report of The Hindu's coverage.

"The entire state is burning, and both the Centre and state governments are responsible."

— Saptagiri Ulaka, Congress MP

The violence that prompted the demand

The demand follows a fresh escalation. On October 19, three Meitei men who had gone to collect firewood in the Sunurok area of Imphal East district were killed, triggering sit-ins and rallies across the Imphal Valley; police arrested three Kuki-Zo men in connection with the killings, whom they identified as alleged cadres of a Kuki National Front faction — an attribution the outfit denied, according to Power Corridors. On October 23, protesters marched across five districts toward Lok Bhavan before police detained them amid lathi charges and tear gas. Clashes between Kuki and Naga communities in Kamjong district have added a second front to the unrest. Demonstrators in Imphal — including women vendors from the Khwairamband Ima Keithel market, student groups and civil society organisations — have separately demanded the resignations of both the Chief Minister and Deputy Chief Minister Nemcha Kipgen, whose planned return to Imphal has been put off because her presence in the capital could become a flashpoint.

What Congress is asking for

Beyond the resignation, the party's demands are specific: time-bound investigations into arson, firing and property destruction; protection for civilians; a strict review of the Suspension of Operations agreement that governs armed groups; restoration of free movement between the valley and the hills; and a clear roadmap for the return of displaced families. Mahila Congress president Alka Lamba, after an early-October visit to the state, said the BJP government "has completely failed to stop the violence there" and that those committing violence are not being punished.

The other side, and what is missing

The state government has not announced any leadership change, and the Chief Minister's office had not issued a detailed response to the Congress demands at the time of publication. The broader accountability questions are also older than this week: Congress MP Gaurav Gogoi has separately pressed the Centre on the delayed Judicial Commission of Inquiry report, deaths and conditions in relief camps flagged by the Supreme Court-appointed Justice Gita Mittal Committee, and the Peace Committee proposed by Home Minister Amit Shah in June 2023. Manipur has already seen one chief ministerial resignation — N. Biren Singh's, followed by President's Rule in February 2025 — without the violence ending, which is the history any fresh-elections demand has to answer.

What happens next

Pressure is set to build toward a rally planned for November 1, and the Union government faces mounting calls to set out how it will restore order. Whether Delhi treats the demand as opposition politics or as a governance decision will be signalled by its response to the investigation and rehabilitation asks, which do not require an election to act on.
